authors: Carrère, S., & Gottman, J. M.
title: Predicting divorce among newlyweds from the first three minutes of a marital conflict discussion
finding: In 124 newlywed couples, how the first three minutes of a conflict discussion went (more negative and less positive emotion) predicted which couples divorced over the next six years.
strength: moderate — one research group's observational sample; striking but not widely replicated as a precise predictor

authors: Gottman, J. M., Coan, J., Carrère, S., & Swanson, C.
title: Predicting marital happiness and stability from newlywed interactions
venue: Journal of Marriage and the Family, 60(1), 5–22
finding: In a six-year study of newlyweds, husbands who accepted influence from their wives were more likely to have stable, happy marriages, while active-listening style paraphrasing during conflict was rare and did not predict outcomes.
strength: moderate — one lab's observational sample of heterosexual newlyweds; the active-listening finding was debated

authors: Driver, J. L., & Gottman, J. M.
title: Daily marital interactions and positive affect during marital conflict among newlywed couples
finding: Observing 49 newlywed couples over dinner and in a conflict discussion, the authors linked turning toward each other's everyday bids with more positive emotion (such as humor and affection) during later conflict.
strength: moderate — observational and correlational, small sample; direction of cause not established

authors: Gottman, J. M., & Levenson, R. W.
title: Marital processes predictive of later dissolution: Behavior, physiology, and health
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 63(2), 221–233
finding: Following 73 couples from 1983 to 1987, couples whose conflict interactions were more negative than positive had more marital problems, lower satisfaction, poorer health and greater risk of separation; physiological arousal was measured alongside behavior.
strength: moderate — influential longitudinal lab study with a small sample

authors: Gottman, J. M.
title: What predicts divorce? The relationship between marital processes and marital outcomes
venue: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates (Hillsdale, NJ); reissued by Routledge
finding: Summarizes Gottman's observational research on couples, including the four horsemen (criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling), the ratio of positive to negative behavior during conflict, and couple types.
strength: moderate — foundational but based on one research program; some reported prediction accuracies were criticized as overfitted

authors: Schrodt, P., Witt, P. L., & Shimkowski, J. R.
title: A meta-analytical review of the demand/withdraw pattern of interaction and its associations with individual, relational, and communicative outcomes
finding: Pooling 74 studies (about 14,000 people), demand/withdraw was moderately associated with poorer relational, communicative and individual outcomes, similarly whichever partner demanded, and more strongly in distressed couples.
strength: strong — large meta-analysis, though the associations are correlational

authors: Christensen, A., Atkins, D. C., Berns, S., Wheeler, J., Baucom, D. H., & Simpson, L. E.
title: Traditional versus integrative behavioral couple therapy for significantly and chronically distressed married couples
venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 72(2), 176–191
finding: In a randomized trial with 134 seriously distressed couples, both integrative (acceptance-based) and traditional behavioral couple therapy produced similar rates of clinically significant improvement, with different patterns of change during treatment.
strength: strong — randomized clinical trial

authors: Christensen, A., Atkins, D. C., Baucom, B., & Yi, J.
title: Marital status and satisfaction five years following a randomized clinical trial comparing traditional versus integrative behavioral couple therapy
venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 78(2), 225–235
finding: Five-year follow-up of the same trial: both therapies helped many couples; integrative therapy showed an advantage in satisfaction through two years of follow-up, with many couples maintaining gains at five years.
strength: strong — long follow-up of a randomized trial

authors: Weger, H., Jr., Castle Bell, G., Minei, E. M., & Robinson, M. C.
title: The relative effectiveness of active listening in initial interactions
finding: People who talked with a listener using active-listening responses felt more understood than those who received advice or simple acknowledgements; differences in satisfaction and liking were small.
strength: moderate — one experiment with 115 participants and trained confederates, in first meetings rather than close relationships

authors: Kruger, J., Epley, N., Parker, J., & Ng, Z.-W.
title: Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 89(6), 925–936
finding: Across five experiments, people overestimated how well email recipients would detect their tone (such as sarcasm or seriousness), partly because they found it hard to step outside their own perspective.
strength: strong — several experiments, widely cited

authors: Daft, R. L., & Lengel, R. H.
title: Organizational information requirements, media richness and structural design
finding: Proposed media richness theory: richer channels (face to face, then phone, then written) are better suited to ambiguous, equivocal messages.
strength: moderate — influential theory; later research found people adapt to leaner media over time

authors: Gunraj, D. N., Drumm-Hewitt, A. M., Dashow, E. M., Upadhyay, S. S. N., & Klin, C. M.
title: Texting insincerely: The role of the period in text messaging
finding: Short text-message replies ending in a period were rated as less sincere than the same replies without one; the effect did not appear for handwritten notes.
strength: early — one study with students; later work suggests the effect fades for longer messages

authors: Huang, K., Yeomans, M., Brooks, A. W., Minson, J., & Gino, F.
title: It doesn't hurt to ask: Question-asking increases liking
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113(3), 430–452
finding: In studies of live conversations, people who asked more questions, especially follow-up questions, were better liked by their partners and seen as more responsive.
strength: moderate — several studies; a 2025 correction fixed minor reporting errors but an audit confirmed the conclusions

authors: Lewicki, R. J., Polin, B., & Lount, R. B., Jr.
title: An exploration of the structure of effective apologies
finding: Testing six apology components with 755 participants, acknowledging responsibility was rated most important, then an offer of repair; a request for forgiveness mattered least. Apologies with more components were rated better.
strength: moderate — two studies using written apology statements, so spoken apologies may differ

authors: Frantz, C. M., & Bennigson, C.
title: Better late than early: The influence of timing on apology effectiveness
finding: Apologies that came later in a conflict were more effective than early ones, and this was explained by the hurt person feeling heard and understood first.
strength: early — two small studies (recalled conflicts and a hypothetical scenario)

authors: Kim, P. H., Ferrin, D. L., Cooper, C. D., & Dirks, K. T.
title: Removing the shadow of suspicion: The effects of apology versus denial for repairing competence- versus integrity-based trust violations
finding: Trust was repaired more successfully when people apologized for competence-based violations but denied culpability for integrity-based violations, depending also on later evidence of guilt or innocence.
strength: moderate — two experiments in a job-candidate scenario

authors: Wade, N. G., Hoyt, W. T., Kidwell, J. E. M., & Worthington, E. L., Jr.
title: Efficacy of psychotherapeutic interventions to promote forgiveness: A meta-analysis
venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 82(1), 154–170
finding: Across 54 reports, people in explicit forgiveness interventions reported more forgiveness than untreated controls and than those in other treatments, along with larger improvements in depression, anxiety and hope than no treatment.
strength: strong — meta-analysis, though forgiveness is measured in varied ways

authors: McNulty, J. K.
title: The dark side of forgiveness: The tendency to forgive predicts continued psychological and physical aggression in marriage
finding: In newlywed couples over four years, partners' aggression stayed stable toward more forgiving spouses but declined toward less forgiving ones, suggesting forgiveness can remove consequences that would discourage repeat offending.
strength: moderate — longitudinal, correlational, newlywed sample

authors: McNulty, J. K.
title: Forgiveness in marriage: Putting the benefits into context
finding: Examines whether the benefits of forgiveness in marriage depend on the relationship context (as the title says, putting the benefits into context). Only the citation, not the abstract, was confirmed in search; check details before quoting specifics.
strength: moderate — small longitudinal study; finding described here at summary level only
verified_by: PubMed record PMID 18266545 with DOI 10.1037/0893-3200.22.1.171 shown in search result (search for title)

authors: McNulty, J. K., O'Mara, E. M., & Karney, B. R.
title: Benevolent cognitions as a strategy of relationship maintenance: "Don't sweat the small stuff"... but it is not all small stuff
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(4), 631–646
finding: Studies of newlyweds on benevolent (generous) interpretations of a partner's behavior; as the title indicates, such interpretations help with small problems but not with serious ones. Only the title and PubMed record were confirmed in search.
strength: moderate — longitudinal newlywed studies

authors: Christensen, A., & Heavey, C. L.
title: Gender and social structure in the demand/withdraw pattern of marital conflict
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59(1), 73–81
finding: Wife-demand/husband-withdraw was more common overall, but who demanded depended partly on whose issue was being discussed; the authors linked the pattern to social structure (who wants change) as well as gender.
strength: moderate — influential observational study; later work finds topic predicts the demander role about as strongly as gender
verified_by: DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.59.1.73 shown in citing reference (search result); https://www.researchgate.net/publication/20941551_Gender_and_Social_Structure_in_the_DemandWithdraw_Pattern_of_Marital_Conflict

authors: Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N.
title: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
finding: A popular book translating Gottman's research into practice: love maps, fondness and admiration, turning toward bids, accepting influence, solving solvable problems, managing perpetual ones, and shared meaning.
strength: moderate — practice framework drawing on his research rather than separately tested

authors: Gottman, J. M.
title: The Science of Trust: Emotional Attunement for Couples
finding: A book drawing on Gottman's lab research and game theory to argue that trust is built through emotional attunement in everyday moments, and describing how couples can repair it.
strength: moderate — book-length synthesis of one research program

authors: Brown, N. J. L., Sokal, A. D., & Friedman, H. L.
title: The complex dynamics of wishful thinking: The critical positivity ratio
finding: Showed that the mathematical modelling behind the claimed 'critical positivity ratio' (about 2.9 to 1, the so-called Losada ratio) was unfounded; the original paper's modelling claims were formally withdrawn.
strength: strong — the critique was accepted and the original model retracted

authors: Hazan, C., & Shaver, P.
title: Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511–524
finding: Two questionnaire studies proposed that adult romantic love is an attachment process: the share of adults in each of three attachment styles roughly matched infant figures, and the styles differed in how people experienced love, their views of self and others, and recalled relationships with parents.
strength: strong — landmark paper; self-report and cross-sectional

authors: Bartholomew, K., & Horowitz, L. M.
title: Attachment styles among young adults: A test of a four-category model
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 61(2), 226–244
finding: Proposed and tested a four-category model of adult attachment (secure, preoccupied, dismissing and fearful).
strength: strong — highly influential; later work favors dimensions over categories
verified_by: Citation with DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.61.2.226 shown in reference lists of PubMed-indexed citing papers (e.g. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31523148/)

authors: Brennan, K. A., Clark, C. L., & Shaver, P. R.
title: Self-report measurement of adult attachment: An integrative overview
venue: In J. A. Simpson & W. S. Rholes (Eds.), Attachment Theory and Close Relationships (pp. 46–76). Guilford
finding: A large factor-analytic study of all known self-report adult attachment measures found that they reduce to two broad dimensions: attachment anxiety and avoidance.
strength: strong — the basis of the widely used two-dimension approach; self-report

authors: Fraley, R. C., Hudson, N. W., Heffernan, M. E., & Segal, N.
title: Are adult attachment styles categorical or dimensional? A taxometric analysis of general and relationship-specific attachment orientations
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 109(2), 354–368
finding: Taxometric analyses suggested that adult attachment differences are dimensional (degrees of anxiety and avoidance) rather than distinct types.
strength: strong — large samples; consistent with the field's current consensus

authors: Bowlby, J.
title: Attachment and Loss, Vol. 1: Attachment
venue: Hogarth Press and the Institute of Psycho-Analysis (London) / Basic Books (New York)
finding: The first volume of Bowlby's trilogy, setting out attachment theory: children's bond with caregivers is an evolved system for seeking safety and comfort.
strength: strong — foundational theory, extensively supported in later research

authors: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S.
title: Patterns of Attachment: A Psychological Study of the Strange Situation
finding: Reported the Strange Situation studies of infants and mothers and described secure and insecure attachment patterns.
strength: strong — foundational, widely replicated method

authors: Coan, J. A., Schaefer, H. S., & Davidson, R. J.
title: Lending a hand: Social regulation of the neural response to threat
finding: In an fMRI study, married women facing the threat of a mild shock showed less threat-related brain activity while holding their husband's hand than when alone.
strength: moderate — small, much-cited brain-imaging study
verified_by: DOI shown in citing references on journals.sagepub.com (e.g. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1948550616646427)

authors: Impett, E. A., Park, H. G., & Muise, A.
title: Popular psychology through a scientific lens: Evaluating love languages from a relationship science perspective
finding: Reviewing the evidence, the authors concluded that the core assumptions of the five love languages (that people have one primary language and that matching languages improves relationships) are not well supported, while its underlying message of learning what a partner needs is sound.
strength: strong — peer-reviewed review of the evidence

authors: Chapman, G.
title: The Five Love Languages: How to Express Heartfelt Commitment to Your Mate
venue: Northfield Publishing (Chicago); later editions retitled The 5 Love Languages
finding: A counselor's book proposing five ways people express and prefer to receive love: words of affirmation, acts of service, receiving gifts, quality time and physical touch. It came from counseling experience, not research.
strength: debated — very popular; research has not supported its core assumptions (see Impett, Park & Muise, 2024)

authors: Chapman, G., & Thomas, J.
title: The Five Languages of Apology: How to Experience Healing in All Your Relationships
venue: Northfield Publishing (Chicago); revised 2022 as The 5 Apology Languages
finding: Proposes that people look for different parts of an apology: expressing regret, accepting responsibility, making restitution, genuinely repenting and requesting forgiveness.
strength: early — popular book with little direct research; Lewicki et al. (2016) tested similar components

authors: Chapman, G., & White, P.
title: The 5 Languages of Appreciation in the Workplace: Empowering Organizations by Encouraging People
finding: Applies the love-languages idea to the workplace, proposing that employees differ in how they prefer to receive appreciation.
strength: early — popular practitioner book with very little independent research
verified_by: Library catalogs list Northfield, Chicago, 2011 (e.g. https://catalog.burlesontx.com/Record/287988 ; https://search.icpl.org/Record/1376580)

authors: Emmons, R. A., & McCullough, M. E.
title: Counting blessings versus burdens: An experimental investigation of gratitude and subjective well-being in daily life
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(2), 377–389
finding: In three studies, people randomly assigned to list things they were grateful for generally reported higher well-being than comparison groups, though not on every measure; effects on positive mood were the most consistent.
strength: moderate — classic experiments; later meta-analyses find small average effects

authors: Algoe, S. B.
title: Find, remind, and bind: The functions of gratitude in everyday relationships
finding: Sets out find-remind-and-bind theory: gratitude helps people find good relationship partners, reminds them of existing good relationships, and binds them closer, by fueling cycles of mutually responsive behavior.
strength: moderate — theory paper drawing on diary, observational and some experimental studies

authors: Algoe, S. B., Gable, S. L., & Maisel, N. C.
title: It's the little things: Everyday gratitude as a booster shot for romantic relationships
finding: In a daily-diary study of cohabiting couples, feeling gratitude after a partner's thoughtful act predicted greater relationship connection and satisfaction the next day, for both partners.
strength: moderate — daily diary, correlational

authors: Gordon, A. M., Impett, E. A., Kogan, A., Oveis, C., & Keltner, D.
title: To have and to hold: Gratitude promotes relationship maintenance in intimate bonds
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(2), 257–274
finding: Across cross-sectional, daily, observational and longitudinal studies, people who felt appreciated by their partners were more appreciative in return; appreciative partners were more responsive and committed, and more likely to still be together months later.
strength: moderate — multi-method but mostly correlational

authors: Dickens, L. R.
title: Using gratitude to promote positive change: A series of meta-analyses investigating the effectiveness of gratitude interventions
finding: A series of meta-analyses (38 studies) found gratitude interventions improved outcomes such as happiness compared with neutral conditions, with smaller or no advantages over other positive activities; the author suggested their unique benefits may be overemphasized.
strength: strong — meta-analysis; effects generally small

authors: Davis, D. E., Choe, E., Meyers, J., Wade, N., Varjas, K., Gifford, A., Quinn, A., Hook, J. N., Van Tongeren, D. R., Griffin, B. J., & Worthington, E. L., Jr.
title: Thankful for the little things: A meta-analysis of gratitude interventions
finding: A meta-analysis found gratitude interventions had small benefits for well-being compared with measurement-only controls and with alternative activities, with mixed results on other outcomes.
strength: strong — meta-analysis; effects small

authors: Gable, S. L., Reis, H. T., Impett, E. A., & Asher, E. R.
title: What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228–245
finding: Across four studies, telling others about good news was linked with higher daily positive mood and well-being beyond the event itself, especially when the listener responded actively and constructively; couples whose partners usually responded enthusiastically reported more intimacy and satisfaction.
strength: strong — multiple studies, widely replicated; mostly correlational

authors: Gable, S. L., Gonzaga, G. C., & Strachman, A.
title: Will you be there for me when things go right? Supportive responses to positive event disclosures
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 91(5), 904–917
finding: In 79 dating couples filmed sharing recent events, how partners responded to good news predicted relationship well-being and break-ups two months later more strongly than how they responded to bad news.
strength: moderate — observational study with a modest sample

authors: Brickman, P., & Campbell, D. T.
title: Hedonic relativism and planning the good society
venue: In M. H. Appley (Ed.), Adaptation-Level Theory (pp. 287–302). Academic Press
finding: Introduced the idea later called the hedonic treadmill: people adapt to improved circumstances, so gains in happiness tend to fade.
strength: moderate — influential theory; later research shows adaptation is real but often incomplete and varies by event

authors: Lyubomirsky, S.
title: Hedonic adaptation to positive and negative experiences
venue: In S. Folkman (Ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Stress, Health, and Coping (pp. 200–224). Oxford University Press (online 2010)
finding: Reviews evidence that both joys and sorrows fade over time, discusses why people may adapt differently to positive and negative changes, and presents a model of how adaptation to positive changes might be slowed.
strength: moderate — narrative review
verified_by: https://sonjalyubomirsky.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Lyubomirsky-2011.pdf ; Oxford Handbooks Online DOI 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780195375343.013.0011 shown in search result

authors: Aron, A., Norman, C. C., Aron, E. N., McKenna, C., & Heyman, R. E.
title: Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273–284
finding: Couples who took part together in a novel, mildly challenging activity reported higher relationship quality afterward than couples who did a mundane task.
strength: moderate — experiments with short-term lab effects; later studies mostly supportive
verified_by: DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.78.2.273 shown in citing reference lists; cited in https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42193579/

authors: Aron, A., & Aron, E. N.
title: Love and the Expansion of Self: Understanding Attraction and Satisfaction
finding: Introduced the self-expansion model: people are motivated to grow by including a partner's perspectives, resources and identity in their sense of self.
strength: moderate — influential theory with broad later support

authors: Hopper, R., Knapp, M. L., & Scott, L.
title: Couples' personal idioms: Exploring intimate talk
finding: An exploratory study of the private words, nicknames and phrases couples develop (personal idioms) and what they are used for in intimate talk.
strength: early — descriptive, exploratory study

authors: Bruess, C. J. S., & Pearson, J. C.
title: 'Sweet pea' and 'pussy cat': An examination of idiom use and marital satisfaction over the life cycle
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 10(4), 609–615
finding: In 154 married couples, more satisfied spouses reported using more private idioms; idiom use was highest early in marriage and declined across the life cycle.
strength: early — one correlational study using recalled idioms

authors: Bruess, C. J. S., & Pearson, J. C.
title: Interpersonal rituals in marriage and adult friendship
finding: Interviews and questionnaires with married couples produced typologies of the everyday rituals people share in marriage (seven types) and in adult friendship (six types).
strength: early — descriptive, qualitative study

authors: Fiese, B. H., Tomcho, T. J., Douglas, M., Josephs, K., Poltrock, S., & Baker, T.
title: A review of 50 years of research on naturally occurring family routines and rituals: Cause for celebration?
finding: A review of 32 publications found family routines and rituals were related to parenting competence, children's adjustment and marital satisfaction, while noting weak measurement and convenience samples.
strength: moderate — qualitative review of mostly correlational studies

authors: Rusbult, C. E.
title: Commitment and satisfaction in romantic associations: A test of the investment model
finding: Two studies tested the investment model: commitment to a relationship was predicted by satisfaction, the quality of alternatives and the size of investments.
strength: strong — foundational, later confirmed by meta-analyses

authors: Le, B., & Agnew, C. R.
title: Commitment and its theorized determinants: A meta-analysis of the Investment Model
finding: A meta-analysis of 52 studies (11,582 participants) found satisfaction, quality of alternatives and investments each correlated with commitment, together explaining about two-thirds of its variance; commitment in turn predicted break-up.
strength: strong — meta-analysis, updated by Tran et al. (2019) with similar conclusions

authors: Rempel, J. K., Holmes, J. G., & Zanna, M. P.
title: Trust in close relationships
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 49(1), 95–112
finding: Described trust in close relationships as having three components, predictability, dependability and faith, and developed a self-report Trust Scale to measure them.
strength: strong — landmark, highly cited model and measure

authors: Murray, S. L., Holmes, J. G., & Griffin, D. W.
title: The self-fulfilling nature of positive illusions in romantic relationships: Love is not blind, but prescient
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 71(6), 1155–1180
finding: Following dating couples over a year, relationships were most likely to last, even through conflicts and doubts, when partners idealized each other most; idealization predicted later gains in satisfaction and fewer conflicts.
strength: moderate — longitudinal but correlational; later work shows limits when problems are serious
note: Replaces the companion paper 'The benefits of positive illusions' (JPSP 70(1)), which could not be confirmed in search.

authors: Drigotas, S. M., Rusbult, C. E., Wieselquist, J., & Whitton, S. W.
title: Close partner as sculptor of the ideal self: Behavioral affirmation and the Michelangelo phenomenon
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(2), 293–323
finding: Across four studies, people whose partners saw and treated them in line with their ideal self moved closer to that ideal over time, and this affirmation was linked with better couple functioning and more stable relationships.
strength: moderate — correlational and longitudinal, not experimental

authors: Ross, L.
title: The intuitive psychologist and his shortcomings: Distortions in the attribution process
finding: Reviewed the biases of the lay 'intuitive psychologist' and named the fundamental attribution error: underestimating situational causes and overestimating personal dispositions when explaining others' behavior.
strength: strong — foundational and widely replicated, though weaker in some cultures

authors: Jones, E. E., & Harris, V. A.
title: The attribution of attitudes
finding: In three experiments, people judged a speaker's true attitude from a speech; they tended to attribute the stated position to the speaker even when told the speaker had been assigned it.
strength: strong — classic, widely replicated paradigm

authors: Jones, E. E., & Nisbett, R. E.
title: The actor and the observer: Divergent perceptions of the causes of behavior
finding: Proposed the actor-observer hypothesis: people tend to explain their own actions by the situation and others' actions by their dispositions.
strength: debated — Malle's 2006 meta-analysis found little overall support for the general claim

authors: Malle, B. F.
title: The actor-observer asymmetry in attribution: A (surprising) meta-analysis
finding: A meta-analysis of 173 studies found average actor-observer effects near zero; the asymmetry appeared only in some conditions (for example when actor and observer were intimates, or for negative events), with a reverse pattern for positive events.
strength: strong — large meta-analysis

authors: Ross, L., & Ward, A.
title: Naive realism in everyday life: Implications for social conflict and misunderstanding
venue: In E. S. Reed, E. Turiel, & T. Brown (Eds.), Values and Knowledge (pp. 103–135). Lawrence Erlbaum / Psychology Press
finding: Described naive realism: people assume they see the world objectively, so those who disagree must be uninformed, irrational or biased — a dynamic that fuels conflict and misunderstanding.
strength: strong — foundational account; its predictions are well replicated

authors: Pronin, E., Lin, D. Y., & Ross, L.
title: The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others
finding: People, from students to airport travelers, readily saw common biases in others but rated themselves as less biased than their peers (the bias blind spot).
strength: strong — replicated in many later studies
verified_by: DOI shown in search results citing the paper (e.g. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/23970022221094523)

authors: Gilovich, T., Savitsky, K., & Medvec, V. H.
title: The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(2), 332–346
finding: In several sets of studies, people overestimated how well others could read their internal states (for example, liars overestimated how detectable their lies were, and people thought their disgust showed more than it did).
strength: strong — replicated and extended

authors: Savitsky, K., Keysar, B., Epley, N., Carter, T., & Swanson, A.
title: The closeness-communication bias: Increased egocentrism among friends versus strangers
finding: In three experiments, people overestimated how well they communicated with friends and spouses, more than with strangers, and made more egocentric errors following a friend's directions; closeness seemed to relax the checking people do with strangers.
strength: moderate — short report of three small experiments; later work extended it

authors: Eyal, T., Steffel, M., & Epley, N.
title: Perspective mistaking: Accurately understanding the mind of another requires getting perspective, not taking perspective
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(4), 547–571
finding: As the title states, a series of experiments found that imagining another person's perspective did not make people more accurate about what that person thought or felt, whereas getting their perspective directly (by asking) did.
strength: strong — many experiments in one paper
verified_by: DOI 10.1037/pspa0000115 shown in reference lists in search results (abstract not retrieved)

authors: Epley, N.
title: Mindwise: How We Understand What Others Think, Believe, Feel, and Want
finding: A book reviewing research on how people infer others' thoughts and feelings, and why this 'sixth sense' is more error-prone than we believe.
strength: moderate — popular book summarizing peer-reviewed research

authors: Hastorf, A. H., & Cantril, H.
title: They saw a game: A case study
venue: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 49(1), 129–134
finding: Students from Princeton and Dartmouth watched the same rough football game and saw it very differently, for example in how many infractions each team committed.
strength: moderate — classic single case study, widely cited
verified_by: DOI shown in search result reference (psycnet citing documents)

authors: Hall, J. A.
title: How many hours does it take to make a friend?
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 36(4), 1278–1296 (online first 2018)
finding: Studies of adults who had recently moved and of students found that more hours spent together, especially in leisure, went with moving from acquaintance to closer friendship.
strength: moderate — survey studies; hour estimates are rough

authors: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B.
title: Social relationships and mortality risk: A meta-analytic review
finding: A meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 participants) found people with stronger social relationships had about 50% greater odds of survival over the study periods, consistently across age, sex and health status.
strength: strong — large meta-analysis of observational studies; causation not established

authors: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., Baker, M., Harris, T., & Stephenson, D.
title: Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: A meta-analytic review
finding: A meta-analysis linking loneliness, social isolation and living alone with a higher risk of earlier death.
strength: strong — meta-analysis of observational studies
verified_by: PubMed citation with DOI 10.1177/1745691614568352, PMID 25910392 shown in search result

authors: Cacioppo, J. T., & Patrick, W.
title: Loneliness: Human Nature and the Need for Social Connection
finding: A book arguing that loneliness is a biological signal, like hunger, that we need connection, and that chronic loneliness can trap people in isolation and harm health.
strength: moderate — popular book summarizing the authors' and others' research

authors: Russell, D., Peplau, L. A., & Ferguson, M. L.
title: Developing a measure of loneliness
finding: Introduced the original 20-item UCLA Loneliness Scale, which showed high internal consistency and links with self-reported loneliness; it was later revised.
strength: strong — the most widely used loneliness measure (in revised forms)

authors: Masi, C. M., Chen, H.-Y., Hawkley, L. C., & Cacioppo, J. T.
title: A meta-analysis of interventions to reduce loneliness
finding: A meta-analysis of loneliness interventions; it is cited for finding that approaches targeting unhelpful social thinking (maladaptive social cognition) showed larger effects than other approaches, and for calling for better-controlled trials.
strength: strong — meta-analysis, though many included studies were small
verified_by: PubMed-style citation with DOI 10.1177/1088868310377394 and PMID 20716644 shown in search result; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1745691615570616 (citing review)

authors: Office of the U.S. Surgeon General (Murthy, V. H.)
title: Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory on the Healing Effects of Social Connection and Community
venue: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
finding: A U.S. public-health advisory reporting that about half of U.S. adults experience measurable loneliness, linking poor social connection with higher risks of heart disease, stroke, dementia and early death, and proposing a national strategy to strengthen connection.
strength: strong — official synthesis of research, though most underlying evidence is observational

authors: Dunbar, R. I. M.
title: Neocortex size as a constraint on group size in primates
finding: Across primates, typical group size was predicted by relative neocortex size rather than by ecological variables; extrapolating to humans gave a rough group size of about 150, the origin of 'Dunbar's number'.
strength: debated — influential; the human extrapolation has wide uncertainty and has been challenged (Lindenfors et al., 2021)

authors: Lindenfors, P., Wartel, A., & Lind, J.
title: 'Dunbar's number' deconstructed
finding: Reanalysing primate brain and group-size data with modern methods gave estimates for human group size that varied widely with method and had very wide confidence intervals, so a specific figure like 150 is not supported.
strength: moderate — methodological reanalysis; Dunbar and colleagues have disputed it

authors: Oswald, D. L., Clark, E. M., & Kelly, C. M.
title: Friendship maintenance: An analysis of individual and dyad behaviors
venue: Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 23(3), 413–441
finding: Three studies identified four kinds of friendship maintenance behavior (positivity, supportiveness, openness and interaction); best friends did more of them, and both friends' maintenance predicted satisfaction and commitment.
strength: moderate — survey studies, mostly students

authors: Granovetter, M. S.
title: The strength of weak ties
finding: Argued that weak ties (acquaintances) are valuable because they bridge between close-knit groups and carry new information, for example about jobs.
strength: strong — one of the most cited papers in sociology; supported by later work including a large 2022 experiment

authors: Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W.
title: Social interactions and well-being: The surprising power of weak ties
finding: Students were happier and felt more belonging on days they interacted with more classmates than usual, and in community samples interactions with weak ties as well as close ties were linked with daily well-being.
strength: moderate — diary studies, correlational

authors: Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W.
title: Is efficiency overrated? Minimal social interactions lead to belonging and positive affect
finding: People who had a brief, friendly social exchange with a coffee-shop barista reported more belonging and positive mood than those who kept the exchange purely efficient.
strength: early — one small field experiment

authors: Epley, N., & Schroeder, J.
title: Mistakenly seeking solitude
finding: Commuters asked to talk with a stranger on their train or bus reported a more positive journey than those told to sit in solitude, even though people predicted the opposite; misjudging how pleasant such talk would be keeps people apart.
strength: moderate — field and lab experiments; replicated in later work
verified_by: DOI shown in citing references in search result (e.g. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34618536/)

authors: Rajkumar, K., Saint-Jacques, G., Bojinov, I., Brynjolfsson, E., & Aral, S.
title: A causal test of the strength of weak ties
finding: Randomized experiments on LinkedIn's 'People You May Know' feature, covering over 20 million users, found that moderately weak ties were most valuable for job mobility, with diminishing returns for the very weakest ties.
strength: strong — large-scale randomized experiments, though on one platform

authors: Bolger, N., Zuckerman, A., & Kessler, R. C.
title: Invisible support and adjustment to stress
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 953–961
finding: In couples where one partner faced a stressful exam, support the recipient did not notice (reported by the giver but not the receiver) was linked with better adjustment, while noticed (visible) support was not.
strength: moderate — diary study; later work shows effects depend on how support is given
verified_by: DOI shown in reference lists of PubMed-indexed citing studies (e.g. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35373659/)

authors: Cohen, S., & Wills, T. A.
title: Stress, social support, and the buffering hypothesis
finding: A review arguing that social support protects (buffers) people from the harmful effects of stress, especially perceived availability of support, alongside general main effects of being socially integrated.
strength: strong — highly influential review; later tests are mixed in some settings
verified_by: DOI shown in reference lists in search results (e.g. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32836986/)

authors: House, J. S.
title: Work Stress and Social Support
finding: A book on social support at work that distinguished emotional, instrumental, informational and appraisal support.
strength: moderate — widely used framework

authors: Flynn, F. J., & Lake, V. K. B. (Vanessa Bohns)
title: If you need help, just ask: Underestimating compliance with direct requests for help
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 95(1), 128–143
finding: People asking for help underestimated, by as much as 50%, how many others would agree to a direct request, because they overlooked how awkward it feels to say no.
strength: strong — several experiments and field studies, widely replicated since

authors: Baumeister, R. F., & Leary, M. R.
title: The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation
finding: A major review arguing that the need to belong is a fundamental human motivation: people need frequent, pleasant contact within a few stable, caring relationships, and unmet belonging has wide emotional and cognitive costs.
strength: strong — highly influential review
verified_by: DOI shown in search result references (e.g. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27134325/)

authors: Kurtz, L. E., & Algoe, S. B.
title: Putting laughter in context: Shared laughter as behavioral indicator of relationship well-being
finding: In 71 couples filmed talking about how they met, the share of time partners spent laughing together (beyond laughter overall) went with higher relationship quality, closeness and perceived support.
strength: moderate — one observational study, correlational

authors: Shenk, C. E., & Fruzzetti, A. E.
title: The impact of validating and invalidating responses on emotional reactivity
venue: Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 30(2), 163–183
finding: In a lab stress task, people who received invalidating responses showed more negative emotion, higher heart rate and higher skin conductance over time than those who received validating responses.
strength: moderate — lab experiment

authors: Gordon, T.
title: P.E.T.: Parent Effectiveness Training
finding: A parenting book and course that popularized 'I-messages': describing your own feelings and the effect of a behavior rather than blaming the other person.
strength: mixed — widely taught; research on I-statements finds tone and context matter as much as wording

authors: Rosenberg, M. B.
title: Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Compassion (later editions: A Language of Life)
finding: Describes Nonviolent Communication: expressing observations, feelings, needs and requests, and listening for the same in others.
strength: early — widely used practice; few rigorous studies
verified_by: Bookseller and library records: 1999 PuddleDancer first edition titled 'A Language of Compassion' (https://www.abebooks.com/first-edition/Nonviolent-Communication-Language-Compassion-Marshall-Rosenberg/31730622023/bd); later editions 'A Language of Life' (2003 2nd ed.; 3rd ed. https://www.harvard.com/book/9781892005281)

authors: Stone, D., Patton, B., & Heen, S.
title: Difficult Conversations: How to Discuss What Matters Most
finding: A practitioner book from the Harvard Negotiation Project describing three conversations inside every hard conversation (what happened, feelings, identity) and the gap between intent and impact.
strength: moderate — practice framework grounded in negotiation experience, not controlled studies

authors: Markman, H. J., Stanley, S. M., & Blumberg, S. L.
title: Fighting for Your Marriage: Positive Steps for Preventing Divorce and Preserving a Lasting Love
finding: A book based on the PREP couples program, teaching skills such as the speaker-listener technique for safer conflict.
strength: moderate — PREP has been tested in trials with some positive and some mixed long-term results

authors: Fisher, R., & Ury, W. (later editions with Patton, B.)
title: Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In
venue: Houghton Mifflin (Boston); 2nd ed. 1991 and 3rd ed. 2011 with Bruce Patton (Penguin)
finding: Set out principled negotiation: separate people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain, use objective criteria, and know your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA).
strength: moderate — very influential practitioner framework informed by research; critics note it can underplay power differences

authors: Baumeister, R. F., Stillwell, A., & Wotman, S. R.
title: Victim and perpetrator accounts of interpersonal conflict: Autobiographical narratives about anger
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59(5), 994–1005
finding: People wrote stories about a time they angered someone and a time someone angered them; perpetrators and victims described the same kinds of event very differently, for example in how serious, understandable and finished the harm was.
strength: moderate — classic narrative study, self-reported memories
verified_by: DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.59.5.994 shown in reference lists in search results (e.g. https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/1994-98807-000-BKM.pdf)

authors: Eubanks, C. F., Muran, J. C., & Safran, J. D.
title: Alliance rupture repair: A meta-analysis
finding: Across 11 studies (1,314 patients), repairing ruptures in the therapist-client relationship was moderately associated with better outcomes; training therapists in rupture repair did not show a significant effect on outcomes in 6 studies.
strength: strong — meta-analysis, correlational for the main finding

authors: Schegloff, E. A., Jefferson, G., & Sacks, H.
title: The preference for self-correction in the organization of repair in conversation
finding: Analyses of everyday conversation showed that 'repair' of trouble in speaking, hearing and understanding is a built-in, organized part of talk, and that people strongly prefer to correct themselves rather than be corrected.
strength: strong — foundational conversation-analysis finding

authors: Jiang, L. C., & Hancock, J. T.
title: Absence makes the communication grow fonder: Geographic separation, interpersonal media, and intimacy in dating relationships
finding: A diary study found long-distance dating couples disclosed more and idealized each other more than geographically close couples, which helped them feel as intimate or more so, with effects varying by communication medium.
strength: early — one diary study of student couples

authors: Roberts, J. A., & David, M. E.
title: My life has become a major distraction from my cell phone: Partner phubbing and relationship satisfaction among romantic partners
finding: In surveys of adults in romantic relationships, a partner's phone snubbing (phubbing) was linked with more conflict over phone use and, through that, lower relationship satisfaction, and indirectly with lower life satisfaction and more depressive symptoms.
strength: moderate — cross-sectional surveys; replicated in several later studies

authors: Bradbury, T. N., & Fincham, F. D.
title: Attributions in marriage: Review and critique
finding: A review finding that distressed spouses explain their partner's negative behavior in more blaming, global and stable ways than satisfied spouses, with experimental, clinical and longitudinal evidence suggesting these attributions may affect satisfaction.
strength: strong — influential review; later longitudinal work suggests effects run both ways

authors: Eidelson, R. J., & Epstein, N.
title: Cognition and relationship maladjustment: Development of a measure of dysfunctional relationship beliefs
venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 50(5), 715–720
finding: Developed the Relationship Belief Inventory, a measure of unrealistic relationship beliefs (such as 'disagreement is destructive' or 'partners should read each other's minds'), which were linked with lower relationship satisfaction.
strength: moderate — widely used measure; correlational findings
verified_by: DOI shown in search result summary of citing records (https://mro.massey.ac.nz/handle/10179/10857 ; https://psytests.org/cbt/relbien.html)

authors: Reis, H. T., & Shaver, P.
title: Intimacy as an interpersonal process

authors: Cutrona, C. E., & Russell, D. W.
title: Type of social support and specific stress: Toward a theory of optimal matching
venue: In B. R. Sarason, I. G. Sarason, & G. R. Pierce (Eds.), Social Support: An Interactional View (pp. 319–366). Wiley

authors: Rogers, C. R., & Farson, R. E.
title: Active Listening
venue: Industrial Relations Center, University of Chicago (essay; widely reprinted)
note: Not verified as linkable: The 1957 essay is confirmed by bookseller/reprint listings (Mockingbird Press reprint, 2021) but no original-publication record or stable reader link was found.
